title: The EU Is About to Restrict the Raw Materials India Needs Most. New Delhi Is Scrambling for Exemptions.
excerpt: Europe's planned ban on metal scrap exports to non-OECD countries and its 47% cut to tariff-free steel imports could raise costs for Indian manufacturers — just as a landmark trade deal between the two is set to take effect.
body:
India and the European Union signed a landmark trade deal earlier this year — the kind of agreement that's supposed to open doors and reduce friction. But before the ink is even dry, two separate EU policy moves are threatening to slam those doors shut for India's most critical industrial sectors.

The first: a planned ban on exporting metal scrap to non-OECD countries. The second: a sweeping overhaul of steel import quotas that slashes tariff-free volumes by 47%. Together, they could raise costs for Indian manufacturers, tighten supply chains, and undermine the very trade pact meant to bring the two economies closer.

India has formally requested exemptions. Brussels hasn't said yes.

The Scrap Problem

Starting May 2027, the EU's revised waste shipment regulation will bar exports of non-hazardous waste — including valuable metal scrap — to countries outside the OECD, unless the EU grants individual country approvals by November 2026. India is not an OECD member.

For Indian steelmakers, this is a supply crisis in the making. The EU is a key provider of high-quality ferrous scrap — the recycled metal that goes into electric arc furnaces and helps India produce steel more cheaply and with lower emissions. India imported roughly 366,000 tonnes of aluminium scrap from the EU in 2025 and was the bloc's top buyer in the first quarter of 2026.

"The EU is a key supplier of high-quality ferrous scrap to India and any export curbs could tighten supply and raise costs for domestic steelmakers," said Pankaj Chadha, chairman of the Engineering Export Promotion Council of India.

Making matters worse, the United Arab Emirates — which supplies about 20% of India's scrap — announced its own export ban in June. If both restrictions take effect, India's recycling-dependent mills will face a double squeeze.

> ""We are providing market participants with predictability through clear and transparent quota distribution rules," said Maros Sefcovic, the EU's top trade negotiator."

The European Commission is also considering separate aluminium scrap export limits, now delayed until September. Industry lobby European Aluminium, which supports curbs, notes that EU aluminium scrap exports hit a record 1.27 million metric tonnes in 2025 — roughly 50% above 2019 levels — with India as the largest destination.

India's trade ministry has formally applied to retain access under the new regime. A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, suggested export quotas rather than a blanket ban could be one compromise. But the clock is ticking: if India doesn't secure approval by November 2026, the door closes.

The Steel Squeeze

In a separate but related move that took effect on Wednesday, the EU overhauled its steel import safeguards. Tariff-free import volumes have been cut by 47%, to 18.3 million tonnes. Any imports above that quota now face a 50% levy across 26 categories of steel products.

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

The EU says the measures protect its steel sector from a 620 million metric tonne global glut, much of it driven by Chinese overproduction. But the restrictions apply to everyone, including trade partners with whom Brussels has free trade agreements.

India is among 13 countries — alongside Turkey, South Korea, and the UK — that receive more favourable terms under the new system. Countries with FTAs will see their tariff-free quotas reduced by roughly one-third, rather than the 47% average. Half of the 18.3 million tonne quota is reserved for FTA partners.

"We are providing market participants with predictability through clear and transparent quota distribution rules," said Maros Sefcovic, the EU's top trade negotiator.

But for India — the world's second-largest crude steel producer — predictability is precisely what's missing. The country's steelmakers export modest volumes to Europe, but those exports have been growing. The new quotas cap that growth potential, even as the trade deal was expected to unlock it.

The Trade Deal Disconnect

The India-EU trade agreement, which was concluded this year, is set to take effect early next year. It does not provide direct relief from EU carbon emission levies — the so-called Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) that will impose costs on imports based on their carbon footprint. And it doesn't address scrap flows or safeguard quotas.

New Delhi expected Brussels to at least avoid steps that would pressure Indian industries while the deal was being implemented. Officials say these scrap and steel restrictions are exactly the kind of friction the agreement was supposed to prevent.

Industry representatives have raised the issue directly with India's trade ministry, according to documents reviewed by Reuters. The ministry has not commented publicly.

What Comes Next

India faces a November 2026 deadline to secure scrap export exemptions — just months before the trade deal is scheduled to go live. Failure would mean Indian steelmakers lose access to European recycled metal at precisely the moment India is trying to scale green steel production.

The aluminium sector faces similar pressure. Vedanta, Hindalco, and National Aluminium Company all depend on scrap imports to supplement domestic supply. Price increases would ripple through construction, automotive, and consumer goods — sectors that directly affect household costs.

For India's diplomatic establishment, the scrap and steel issues represent a test of the broader trade relationship. The EU-India deal was celebrated as a generational achievement. But if its benefits are eroded by parallel restrictions before the first tariff reduction even takes effect, the political appetite for future deals — on both sides — could sour quickly.

The November deadline approaches. And neither side appears to be blinking.

nri_angle: NRIs with business interests in Indian manufacturing or real estate should watch closely — rising steel and aluminium costs could push up construction prices, infrastructure project timelines, and the cost of everything from vehicles to appliances.
